en: *Avataṃsaka-sūtra-śāstra*, Fascicle Three, composed by Master Yuanxiao.
Explaining the "Chapter on the Tathāgata’s Radiance and Enlightenment. Herein, the Tathāgata emits light that universally illumines the ten directions, causing—
The great assembly eliminates the obscuration of darkness and realizes that the Tathāgata’s body pervades the entire Dharma-realm;
for this reason, it is called the "Chapter on the Enlightenment of Radiance.
The meaning of the answers to these two questions is as previously explained.
Furthermore, this Buddha-light extinguishes all doubts and dispels all calamities;
for this reason, in response to those two phrases, the original state is further established.
Within the section on the division of faith, among the two [parts],
this raises the fruit attained and gives rise to a mind of aspiration and joy.
Having previously [discussed] the second point below— that which is not practiced— regarding the generation of the intent for progress,
the four categories herein are divided into two parts.
That is to say, the first two chapters dispel various doubts and difficulties so as to give rise to faith and understanding;
the latter two chapters [do the same].
This correctly explains the virtues of practice to inspire further cultivation.
This section also has two parts;
the first chapter dispels doubts.
Next is the section on resolving objections.
"Resolving objections" refers to those difficulties regarding the Dharma that are hard to understand,
as they give rise to various challenges.
Those who harbor doubts have not yet placed faith in the Buddha,
for they give rise to various forms of uncertainty. From what cause do these doubts arise?
The preceding two chapters state that the Buddha’s name, being true, is distributed throughout all worlds in the ten directions.
Regarding this, a doubt arises:
Is it because the Buddha’s body is pervasive that his voice follows along and is likewise pervasive?
If the body is localized while this [name] alone is pervasive,
and if the name alone is pervasive while the body is not,
how could the retribution of bodily karma be narrow?
The fruit of the karma of speech is vast,
because the two types of karma originally cultivated are both immeasurable.
If it were as the name suggests— that it pervades the body as well— then [the same would apply].
Why is it that one sees only the Buddha in the world?
This chapter has come forth to dispel this doubt;
such is its general purport.
Next, I shall explain the text, which contains two parts:
first, clarifying the source from which the light emerges;
second, revealing the places illuminated by the light.
At the beginning, it is said that from the wheels on the soles of his two feet, he emits ten billion rays of light.
These wheels are the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel (*sahasrāra-cakra*),
which serves to symbolize faithful practice (*śraddhā-carita*).
As for the initial arousal [of the mind], one first gives rise to ten thoughts,
increasing them to a hundred thousand.
Because it is the entry into the stage of the Worthy One (Śaikṣa) through the simultaneous practice of śamatha and vipaśyanā,
[the light] emerges from the wheels on the soles of his two feet.
From the point where the light of the Universal Illuminator shines downward, from the near to the far, it increases in ten successive layers;
this represents the stages of gradual cultivation and progress that must be fulfilled by those who have first set out on the path.
Herein, it is clearly shown that the Buddha’s body is all-pervasive;
therefore, the karmic retributions of both his bodily and vocal actions are likewise equal, boundless, and coextensive with the Dharma-realm.
Within this first stage, there are two divisions.
First, the events witnessed in the places illuminated by light are described;
subsequently, the exposition of the verses of praise to the Buddha spoken by the Bodhisattva Rucideva is clarified.
Within the former section, there are also two parts.
First, it reveals that the light illuminates ten billion worlds;
subsequently, it clarifies the universal vision of the Buddha and the great assembly.
The same structure applies to the nine successive sections that follow.
Within the praise of the Buddha, there are also two parts:
first, clarifying one location;
second, applying it by analogy to other locations.
There are two [sections] within the verses.
The first two verses praise the Buddha based on the name of the Buddha in the eastern direction:
"Immovable Appearance" (Acalākāra).
The final eight verses are attributed to the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī;
they manifest the wisdom that is non-abiding and non-attaining.
These also consist of two parts.
The first verse reveals through negation (*pratipakṣa*), while the subsequent verses clarify through affirmation (*anuloma*).
As for the meaning revealed through negation: if one knows that the Tathāgata is liberated from bondage and free from [defilements], yet remains full [of virtues].
Then one would say that the Tathāgata has movement and emergence;
since there is something attained, it is not the pure eye.
This accords with the meaning of clarity.
If one knows that the Tathāgata perceives all phenomena as being non-existent,
then one accords with the Tathāgata’s immovable wisdom;
since there is no abiding therein, one swiftly becomes a Buddha.
Within the subsequent eight verses, there are four pairs.
In the first pair, the initial verse realizes that the conventional lacks reality, while the following verse enters into the non-duality of the ultimate.
As for the second pair, the former clarifies that one does not abide in persons.
The third pair first clarifies that regarding the Dharma one is free from existence and non-existence, and subsequently reveals that regarding the Buddha there is neither decrease nor increase.
The fourth "pair-free" [section] first clarifies the gate of non-apprehension regarding persons and dharmas to transform sentient beings.
Subsequently, by manifesting the gate of the non-obstruction between the one and the many, one attains fearlessness.
Because all phenomena enter into a single phenomenon, one understands the infinite within the one;
because a single phenomenon enters into all phenomena, one understands the one within the infinite.
The reason they are able to enter into one another is that they arise through mutual reflection like images in mirrors; because they arise without being real, there is no obstruction.
This is called the Dharma-gate of the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī.
The second verse also consists of two parts;
in the preceding two verses, the names of the Buddhas of the southern direction were invoked to praise the Dharma-gate of the fire of wisdom.
The subsequent eight verses rely upon the names of those bodhisattvas to manifest the Dharma-gate of Bodhiśiras.
Within the first [section], there are two parts.
The first verse shows how one perceives all sentient beings shrouded in the darkness of ignorance and causes them to seek the supreme light of wisdom;
the latter verse shows how one inwardly harbors the fire of unswerving gnosis while outwardly revolving the supreme wheel of light.
Within the subsequent eight verses, there are likewise four pairs.
As for the first pair: the former takes the great vow as its primary focus to awaken those sleeping in the cycle of birth and death;
the latter takes compassion as its core intention to subdue the host of māras and adversaries.
The second pair consists of those who have internally attained profound wisdom-awakening and are able to destroy all afflictions,
and externally strike the drum of the True Dharma to awaken the lands of the ten directions.
The third pair consists of, on the lower level, not grasping at or clinging to anything within all states of existence (*bhava*),
and on the higher level, giving rise to thoughts of joy toward all Buddhas.
The fourth pair consists of undergoing suffering for long eons in order to rescue sentient beings.
To protect the Buddha-dharma,
he does not spare his own body or life;
this is the Dharma-gate of the Bodhisattva Chief of Enlightenment for awakening oneself and awakening others.
The third verse also consists of two parts.
In the preceding verse, the names of Buddhas from the western direction were invoked to praise the practice of pure wisdom and the Dharma.
The subsequent nine verses, based on the name of that Bodhisattva Vasumitra,
clarify the dharma-gate of manifesting various meritorious qualities to benefit all sentient beings.
The beginning and middle consist of two parts:
the first half concerns the purity of awakening,
and the second half concerns the purity of mind.
This is called the practice of the Dharma through pure wisdom.
Within the fourth verse there are also two parts;
in the preceding nine verses, the names of Buddhas from the northern direction are invoked.
This praises the dharma-gate of possessing majestic power, wisdom,
and virtue; the final verse, based on the name of that Bodhisattva Ratnaśrī,
reveals the dharma-gate of purity like refined gold.
The beginning and middle also consist of two parts.
In the preceding verse, the inner and outer perfections of majestic power (*vibhūti*) are indicated in general;
therein, the first half concerns the majestic power of internal realization (*pratyātma-adhigama*).
The final two lines externally manifest majestic power (*vibhūti*).
The subsequent eight verses specifically reveal the perfection of four pairs of majestic powers.
The first pair is the quality of self-awakening free from defilements (*rajas*).
The first pair is the majesty that universally arises to transform others;
the second pair is the majesty of internal liberation and external deliverance, which is free from the aggregates and devoid of suffering;
the third pair is the majesty of being tranquil yet constantly active.
The virtue of being active yet eternally quiescent.
The fourth pair consists of the virtue of skillfully knowing the profound and the majestic power of universally perceiving and extensively delivering.
In the fifth verse, there are likewise two divisions.
In the first five verses, based on the Bodhisattva Guṇasāgarabuddhi,
his merits of self-benefit and benefit for others are elucidated.
In the subsequent five verses, they are presented under the name of the fifth Buddha, Jñānasāgara.
He praises that inconceivable realm of luminous illumination.
This section also consists of two parts;
the first verse concerns the virtue of his compassion in transforming the multitudes of sentient beings below.
The subsequent four verses concern the virtues of seeking the Buddha-way and advancing in practice.
The final five verses are likewise divided into two parts;
the first two verses clarify the realm of contemplating the true nature of body and mind.
The subsequent three verses reach the immeasurable and inconceivable realm.
Within the sixth verse, there are two parts:
six lines of seven-syllable verse.
There are five verses in the five-character style.
Within the seven-character verses, there are also two parts;
the first two verses rely upon the Bodhisattva Mūrdhābhiṣikta (Crown-Consecrated) of the sixth chapter.
By contrast, this reveals the wondrous forms perceived by the Pure Eye.
The final four verses entrust the names of the Buddhas of the southeast to praise the profound and wondrous realm of ultimate wisdom.
Within these five-syllable verses, there are likewise two parts.
The first two verses rely on the names of the eyes and heads to praise the Buddha’s pure eye and the dharma-gate of mastery.
The final three verses address those Buddhas' names and praise the profound realm of ultimate wisdom;
within the seventh verse, there is also a twofold division.
In the preceding two verses,
by invoking the name of the Buddha of the southwest,
the Buddha’s unsurpassed wisdom and awakening are praised.
The subsequent eight verses rely upon the name "Vajragarbha" (Diamond-Womb) to reveal that bodhisattva’s entry into the sphere of the Buddha’s wisdom.
This section also consists of two parts.
The preceding [verses] extol the unsurpassed wisdom that awakens oneself and awakens others;
the subsequent [verses] praise the unsurpassed virtues that are untainted and indestructible.
Within the final eight verses, four pairs of qualities do not appear.
The first pair enters the Buddha’s wisdom and enters the ocean of Dharma.
The second pair correctly turns the wheel of the Dharma and correctly contemplates the path of the Buddha.
The third pair accords with the Buddha’s true teaching and knows the Buddha’s actual virtues.
The fourth pair consists of observing cessation and realizing equality;
this is called the "Foremost Progression" entrance into the Dharma-gate.
Within the eighth verse, there are twenty stanzas.
It is then divided into two parts.
The first ten verses are dedicated to the Buddha residing in the northwest, whose name is [inserted here].
The [first] ten verses praise the power of skillful means (*upāya*) of sovereign wisdom (*jñāna*).
The subsequent ten verses, based on the name "Dharma-Head" (*dharma-mūrdhan*) of the Bodhisattva,
praise the power of wisdom that accords with the meaning of the Dharma.
At the beginning there are five pairs.
The first pair consists of the mastery of great wisdom and the accomplishment of great virtue.
The second pair consists of the vast contemplation of the nature of awakening and the profound delight in being free from signs.
The third pair consists of being unimpeded regarding existence and being unattached to emptiness.
The fourth pair consists of clearly discerning distinctions while delighting in observing equality.
The fifth pair consists of encompassing all-knowledge and accomplishing the supreme intention.
These five pairs and ten gates of skillful means are all manifestations of the differentiation of sovereign wisdom (*vaśitājñāna*).
Next, the wisdom of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) is praised.
There are also five pairs.
The first pair consists of profound knowledge of the Dharma and the thorough knowledge that leads to the ultimate destination.
The second pair consists of compliance with single-mindedness and the ability to reach the profound realm.
The third pair consists of remembering specific times and discerning success and failure.
The fourth pair consists of distinguishing the objects of knowledge and being able to understand the skillful means.
The fifth pair consists of observing the three periods of time and realizing their equality.
These five pairs are all the primary dharma-gates.
Within the ninth verse there are also two parts;
in the preceding ten verses, the names of the Buddhas from that lower direction are enshrined.
He praises the Dharma-gate of the Wisdom of Brahmā with [the first] ten verses;
thereafter, he praises the Dharma-gate of the Lamp of Wisdom that Dispels Darkness based on the name of the Bodhisattva Jñānaśrī.
The beginning and middle consist of two parts:
two verses provide a brief outline,
and eight verses offer a detailed explanation.
Within the headings there are also two parts:
the first clarifies the Brahma-conduct,
and the latter reveals the Brahma-sound.
Regarding the term "brahmacarya":
when Brahmā manifests a transformation-body to appear among humans,
he undergoes the practice of difficult austerities, his form resembling a skeleton.
One should know that the difficult practice is itself the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
The eight verses provide a detailed explanation,
which reveals four gateways.
The first consists of two verses on the Dharma-gate of abandoning arrogance,
which removes the suffering and hardships of birth and death.
The second consists of two verses on the Dharma-gate of heedfulness.
To eliminate worldly negligence,
the third section consists of two verses that proclaim the teaching of non-self (anātman) to extinguish the sentient beings' attachment to a self.
The fourth consists of two verses on the gate of the great vow to universally moisten and extinguish the blazing fires of sentient beings;
this is called the gate of Brahmā’s practice.
Within the subsequent ten verses, there are likewise two parts.
In the preceding two verses, the gateways of wisdom are briefly indicated.
Within these, the first verse identifies the darkness to be extinguished,
while the subsequent seven verses reveal the lamp that can extinguish it.
Within the explanation of these eight verses, there are also four sections:
first, two verses on the dharma-gate of crossing over by boat;
second, two verses on the dharma-gate of rescuing those submerged by means of a bridge.
Third is the dharma-gate of extracting suffering through skillful means in two verses;
fourth is the dharma-gate of bestowing happiness through true wisdom in two verses.
Within the tenth verse, there are likewise two parts.
In the first four verses, he addresses the Buddha of the upper direction by name and extols the dharma-gate of subduing resentment through wisdom;
in the subsequent sixteen verses, he relies upon the name of that bodhisattva, Bhadramukha.
The extensive exposition of the *Bhadramukha-viśeṣa-dharma-paryāya* has two parts in its beginning.
In the first two verses, it correctly reveals the ten powers (*daśabala*), which are the supreme wisdom for subduing adversaries.
The following two verses indicate the name,
fame, and supreme virtues of the Subduer of Enemies (Vajrapāṇi).
From "Universally for the sake of all sentient beings" onwards, [the text] presents the second Dharma-gate, that of Bhadramukha.
Within this, there are two parts:
the first four verses concern the superior capacity for the downward transformation of sentient beings,
and the subsequent twelve verses concern the superior capacity for the upward seeking of the Buddha-way.
"Being able to question the Buddhas of the ten directions" and following constitute the second section on seeking the Buddha-way above.
These twelve verses are combined into six pairs.
The first pair consists of questioning the Buddha and seeing the Buddha.
Second, the ability to teach and the ability to manifest transformations constitute a pair.
Third, hearing the Buddha’s voice and seeing the Buddha’s body constitute a pair.
Fourth, attachment to existence and non-attachment, as well as their opening [to liberation], constitute a pair.
The fifth pair uses lower metaphors to illustrate higher dharmas;
the sixth pair uses external analogies to illustrate internal dharmas.
These latter two pairs rely on the gate of inference (*anumāna*) to establish the meaning that the Buddha-body is all-pervasive.
The preceding ten layers of radiant light universally illuminating manifest that the Buddha’s form-body (rūpakāya) pervades everywhere;
the ten layers of verses praising the Buddha’s merits clarify that the Buddha’s internal virtues likewise reach everywhere without exception.
Regarding the fact that the virtues of the bodhisattvas are also revealed therein:
it clarifies that all bodhisattvas, in accordance with the Buddha, are able to conform to the Buddha;
having given rise to doubts, they have completely eliminated them.
Copied from the Ishimui-in original on the ninth day of the seventh month in the tenth year of Kōwa.
